source.title: OPIUM: Mitigating Steering Externalities and Over-Refusal via Dual Objective Latent Optimization
source.authors: Kavin Aravindan; Arihant Rastogi; Krishak Aneja; Aaditya Prasad; Saiyam Jain; Vaishnavi Shivkumar; P. Kumaraguru

record.tranche_reason: The study reports effects of adding a contrastively extracted refusal vector and of directionally ablating the refusal direction, including incomplete safety restoration and a utility cost. These results refine the scope of the single-direction intervention claim.
record.gate_note: The study directly evaluates a refusal vector on benign and harmful prompts and reports directional-ablation outcomes for safety and utility. OPIUM's own optimization hyperparameter sweeps are not rows because they measure the new optimization method rather than the claim's direction itself. Cited results from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study adds a contrastive refusal vector to two instruct models and reports refusal-related rates on harmful and benign prompts (Table 1). That bears on V1's claim that adding the direction induces refusal. The vector comes from refusal-vs-compliant completions on harmful prompts, not harmful-minus-harmless instructions. It is added at one layer with one strength (α=4). Most of the paper evaluates OPIUM, its own method. The ablation result projects the refusal direction out of a utility vector; it does not ablate it from the model.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with two corrections. OPIUM reduces over-refusal relative to the refusal vector only by partially giving up its safety gain. The directional-ablation critique concerns projecting the refusal direction out of utility steering vectors, not ablating refusal from the model.
record.recipe_differences: The refusal vector is extracted contrastively from harmful prompts with refusal versus compliant completions, then added at one intermediate layer. This is not the original all-layer, all-position ablation procedure; the study also evaluates a directional-ablation comparator.
record.method_sensitivity: For the refusal-vector evaluation, intervention layer differs by model (Layer 18 for Qwen and Layer 13 for Llama). For externality ablation, the text reports incomplete safety restoration on Qwen and a utility cost on Llama. The paper also reports that OPIUM outcomes vary with comparison layer and loss weight, but those are not direct tests of the claim's direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Projecting the refusal direction out of corrigibility/survival-instinct utility steering vectors does not fully restore HarmBench safety on Qwen. On Llama it weakens the intended steering effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety erosion from benign utility steering is not carried solely by the refusal direction's component of the steering vector.

record.peer_reviewed: Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, 2026
record.problems: The refusal-vector results cover two instruct models, a 318-prompt benign subset, and 320 HarmBench prompts; no uncertainty estimates are reported. The study does not test ablation across every layer and position or broad general capability. Directional-ablation results are qualitative in the text, without numerical values there.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant results were left out. OPIUM optimization hyperparameter sweeps in Tables 2 and 3 were omitted because they report performance of the proposed optimization procedure rather than an outcome of the refusal direction itself.

untested.parts: Ablating the direction from the model's activations or weights to remove refusal. The original harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means extraction. Addition on harmless prompts at the strengths used originally. Retention of general capabilities.
All; no jailbreak or adversarial-training analysis.

missing.what: Numeric ASR and utility values for the directional-ablation baseline versus vanilla steering and the base model, per model and behaviour.

record.verdict_notes: The refusal vector is used mainly as a baseline for OPIUM, so its weight as a V1 test is limited. The paper says the refusal vector is applied 'as in Sec 4.2', but the appendices give different Llama settings: layer 13 for over-refusal versus layer 15 with α=2.0 for externality. Benign responses were judged by Gemini 2.5 Flash. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The 318-prompt benign set is a stratified subset of FalseReject.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not ablate the direction from every layer and position, test whether it accounts for all refusal behavior, or assess broad general capability. Its refusal vector is extracted contrastively from harmful prompts with refusal versus compliant completions and applied at an intermediate layer.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration experiment.
No test of attacks suppressing the direction or training against its ablation.
No comparison of a single direction with an affine subspace, cone, or multiple directions.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
No transfer test across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
No comparison of refusal training procedures or training stages.

rows.subject: Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Project the refusal direction out of the utility steering vector
rows.baseline: Vanilla steering; numeric value not stated
rows.value: Directional ablation fails to fully restore safety
rows.note: The text states that projecting out the refusal direction does not fully restore safety on Qwen.
rows.check: The operation projects the refusal direction out of a utility (corrigibility/survival) steering vector; it does not ablate refusal from the model. It therefore cannot show V1's 'ablation removes refusal' effect. It is a baseline compared with OPIUM, and its values are only plotted in Fig. 2.

rows.baseline: Vanilla steering; numeric value not stated
rows.value: Directional ablation sacrifices utility relative to vanilla steering
rows.note: The text explicitly reports a utility cost on Llama; it does not give the plotted numeric value.
rows.check: Here 'utility' means the strength of the target steering behaviour on MCQ items, not general capability. Same projection-from-utility-vector operation as r13; a baseline comparison with no readable numbers.

relationships.condition: Adding the contrastive refusal vector (α=4, single layer) on HarmBench DirectRequest, Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B
relationships.reason: Refusal of harmful prompts rises: ASR falls 32.50→14.06 (Qwen) and 25.31→15.31 (Llama). r3, r6.
relationships.display_finding: Adding the vector reduced ASR from 32.50 to 14.06 in Qwen and from 25.31 to 15.31 in Llama.

relationships.condition: Adding the same vector on benign FalseReject prompts, single layer, α=4
relationships.reason: Induced refusal on benign prompts is modest: non-refusal (USR) drops only about 5–7 points on both models, far from refusing nearly everything. Strength was not swept. r1, r2, r4, r5.
relationships.display_finding: At α=4, non-refusal fell only about 5–7 points in both models.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Standard refusal-vector addition on the two tested instruct models
reader_labels.reason: The refusal vector lowers benign compliance and harmful-prompt ASR on both models, consistent with inducing refusal; see r1–r6.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Directional ablation in the steering-externality settings
reader_labels.reason: Ablation incompletely restores Qwen safety and costs Llama utility, so its effects are not a clean safety-only removal; see r13–r14.
